data.title: M & B Engineering's (NSE:MBEL) Earnings Are Weaker Than They Seem
data.description:
M & B Engineering Limited (NSE:MBEL) just reported some strong earnings, and the market reacted accordingly with a healthy uplift in the share price. However, our analysis suggests that shareholders may be missing some factors that indicate the earnings result was not as good as it looked.

We've found 21 US stocks that are forecast to pay a dividend yield of over 6% next year. See the full list for free.

Zooming In On M & B Engineering's Earnings

In high finance, the key ratio used to measure how well a company converts reported profits into free cash flow (FCF) is the accrual ratio (from cashflow). In plain english, this ratio subtracts FCF from net profit, and divides that number by the company's average operating assets over that period. This ratio tells us how much of a company's profit is not backed by free cashflow.

As a result, a negative accrual ratio is a positive for the company, and a positive accrual ratio is a negative. That is not intended to imply we should worry about a positive accrual ratio, but it's worth noting where the accrual ratio is rather high. To quote a 2014 paper by Lewellen and Resutek, "firms with higher accruals tend to be less profitable in the future".

For the year to September 2026, M & B Engineering had an accrual ratio of 0.37. As a general rule, that bodes poorly for future profitability. And indeed, during the period the company didn't produce any free cash flow whatsoever. Over the last year it actually had negative free cash flow of ₹1.3b, in contrast to the aforementioned profit of ₹1.04b. Coming off the back of negative free cash flow last year, we imagine some shareholders might wonder if its cash burn of ₹1.3b, this year, indicates high risk.

That might leave you wondering what analysts are forecasting in terms of future profitability. Luckily, you can click here to see an interactive graph depicting future profitability, based on their estimates.

Our Take On M & B Engineering's Profit Performance

As we have made quite clear, we're a bit worried that M & B Engineering didn't back up the last year's profit with free cashflow. For this reason, we think that M & B Engineering's statutory profits may be a bad guide to its underlying earnings power, and might give investors an overly positive impression of the company. But the good news is that its EPS growth over the last three years has been very impressive. At the end of the day, it's essential to consider more than just the factors above, if you want to understand the company properly. If you'd like to know more about M & B Engineering as a business, it's important to be aware of any risks it's facing. Case in point: We've spotted 2 warning signs for M & B Engineering you should be mindful of and 1 of them doesn't sit too well with us.

That move jars with the headline numbers. Quarterly revenue reached US$115.8b and basic earnings per share hit US$2.71, while trailing net profit margins sat at a very high 62.5%. "The main thing that has to go right is that NVIDIA continues to scale its full stack AI factory platform with supply constrained demand across hyperscalers and ACIE customers, while managing memory cost pressures and the loss of China data center compute revenue."

Q3 goes a long way toward that objective. Data center revenue of about US$108b, alongside roughly US$20b from Vera Rubin’s first production quarter, indicates broad take up of full systems rather than just chips. ACI&E near US$47b shows the non hyperscaler engine is already material, even as China data center sales are effectively excluded from guidance.

NVIDIA: Bear Fears On Margin Durability Get A Real Test

Q3 reported gross margins around 74.8 to 74.9% and management still points to a Q4 trough at 71 to 72%, so the compression the quote worries about is now explicitly in the outlook. At the same time, trailing net margin at 62.5% remains very high and Q4 revenue is guided up to about US$130b, which means NVIDIA is absorbing higher memory and financing costs without a collapse in earnings power.   • The group closed fiscal 2026 with a record €164b order backlog and plans about €4b of capacity investment by 2030. This highlights how current demand for gas turbines and grid equipment is shaping Siemens Energy’s long term production footprint.
  • This article now explores how Siemens Energy’s change in net income and its record order backlog could influence the investment narrative around the business.

Siemens Energy Investment Narrative Recap

For a shareholder in Siemens Energy, the core belief is that the record order backlog and strong earnings can be turned into reliable cash generation over several years. The recent €3,783 million full year net income and higher earnings per share show the business operating with more financial headroom. The near term swing factor is still execution on large grid and gas turbine projects, while the biggest risk is any meaningful delay or repricing in that backlog.

In the short term, this earnings print does not change what matters most. Siemens Energy still needs to ramp capacity, hold margins in Gas Services and Grid Technologies, and keep Siemens Gamesa on a steadier footing. If cost pressure increases or mix shifts away from higher margin work, the improved group net margin could prove difficult to sustain.

The analyst consensus narrative on Simply Wall St already framed the record order book and capacity expansion plans as key supports for future earnings. The latest report, with €44,243 million in full year sales and €3,783 million in net income, provides additional evidence that Siemens Energy is monetising parts of that pipeline and lifting profitability versus the prior year.

This is relevant for the catalysts built around long running gas turbine and grid contracts. Strong recent earnings, a reported return on equity of 35.2%, and a record €164 billion backlog make execution risk more visible. The key question now is whether Siemens Energy can continue converting that backlog into high quality earnings while managing an unstable dividend record and a share price that has been volatile over the past three months.

Siemens Energy's narrative projects €63.0b revenue and €7.6b earnings by 2029. This hinges on revenue growing by 14.6% per year and earnings increasing by about €4.9b from €2.7b today.
